scenes.explain: Context and reasons let the model make the right call, even in cases the prompt never lists.

items.text: Parts of a prompt: context, task, data, constraints, examples
Context and reasons beat bare rules
Effort and structured outputs replace old tricks

captions.text: Welcome to Module 3.
In Module 2 you learned to call a language model reliably.
Now we make the model do the right thing, consistently.
That's prompt engineering.
Not magic words, but clear writing, structured outputs, and measurement.
By the end of this module you'll build an AI resume analyzer that turns a resume and
a job posting into a skills-gap report.
You'll be able to name the parts of a prompt, and what each part does.
Turn a vague request into a specific one.
State constraints plainly, with the reason behind them.
And recognise prompting advice that current models no longer need.
A good prompt usually has five parts.
Not every prompt needs all five, but knowing them tells you what's missing.
First, context.
Who is the output for, and what happens to it next?
This is the part beginners leave out, and the part that matters most.
Second, the task: one clear sentence saying what to produce.
Third, the data: the document the model works on, kept clearly separate from your
instructions.
Fourth, constraints: what counts, what doesn't, and the shape of the answer.
And fifth, examples, when the format or the judgment is subtle.
We'll cover those in the next lesson.
Here are two prompts for the same task, both from this module's project.
The first one is how most people start: a generic role, and one short instruction.
It isn't wrong, but it leaves every decision to the model.
Which skills count?
Soft skills too?
In what format?
Should it guess skills the resume only implies?
The second version says who uses the output, and what happens to it: code compares
it with a job posting.
That one sentence explains why accuracy matters more than completeness, so the model
can make the right call in situations the prompt never mentions.
Context is the cheapest improvement you can make.
Say who the output is for, and how it will be used.
Describe the quality bar: what does a great answer look like?
And explain the reason behind each rule.
A rule with a reason generalises to cases you never thought of.
A bare rule doesn't.
When a prompt is too short, the model fills the gaps with safe defaults, and you get
generic output.
Give more context than seems necessary.
You'll find prompts full of capital letters: critical, must, never, important.
That style was written for older models that sometimes ignored instructions.
Current models follow instructions closely, so shouting makes them over-apply the
rule, and stacked prohibitions can even pull them toward the very mistake you
mention.
Instead, state the rule once, in a normal voice, say exactly what counts, and give
the reason.
A concrete edge case, like "no experience with Kubernetes", is worth more than any
number of capital letters.
Prompting advice ages quickly.
Here are four patterns you'll still see in tutorials, and what to use instead on
current Claude models.
Think step by step.
Current models already reason before they answer, and you control how much with the
effort setting from Module 2, not with prose.
Reply only in JSON, followed by regular expressions to dig the JSON out.
Use structured outputs instead: the API constrains the reply to your schema.
That's lesson three.
Prefilling, where you start the assistant's reply for it, is rejected with a four
hundred error on current Claude models.
Structured outputs replace it.
And don't add a reasoning field to your JSON for the model to fill in.
If you need to know why, ask for a short explanation of the answer.
Is the longer prompt expensive?
This script renders both versions for a short resume.
Version two is about two hundred tokens longer.
At four dollars per million input tokens, that's less than a tenth of a cent per
call.
Input tokens are cheap, and wrong answers are not.
Quick check.
Which change most improves a vague prompt?
Saying who uses the output, and why accuracy matters.
Context and reasons let the model make good decisions in cases you never listed.
A prompt has context, a task, data, constraints, and sometimes examples.
Context and reasons beat bare rules.
Write in plain language, at normal volume.
And use effort and structured outputs, not old tricks.
Next lesson: examples, separating data from instructions with tags, and splitting a
big task into smaller steps.
